successor: Kingdom of England under William III and Mary II (British Empire I)
source2: The National Archives (UK), 'Glorious Revolution' education resource - https://www.nationalarchives.gov.uk/education/resources/glorious-revolution/
notes: Invited Dutch landing (Nov 1688) and James II's flight changed ruler, but Crown, Parliament and law continued; Convention Parliament offered crown Feb 1689. T2 reading arguable (William's army). Q4: Monmouth 1685, Civil Wars 1642-51. Tudor start 1485.

source1: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History, 'Ife' - https://www.metmuseum.org/toah/hd/ife/hd_ife.htm
notes: Ooni kingship and city persisted; Britannica: as Ife's power declined its administrative arrangements continued. 1400 is a periodisation boundary; Met dates flourishing c.1200-1500. Reported 14th-15th c. epidemic or Owu war not verified; possible depopulation debated.

successor: Western Han (Liu Bang); briefly Xiang Yu's settlement
source1: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'China: The Qin empire (221-207 BCE)' - https://www.britannica.com/place/China/The-Qin-empire-221-207-bce
source2: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline, 'Han Dynasty (206 B.C.-220 A.D.)' - https://www.metmuseum.org/toah/hd/hand/hd_hand.htm
notes: Revolts from 209 BCE spread as old elites of six states rose; rebel Liu Bang (ex-Qin official) took last Qin ruler's surrender (207/206). Rebels inside realm, so internal. Civil war; Han reunified 202.

source1: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'China: The end of Mongol rule' - https://www.britannica.com/place/China/The-end-of-Mongol-rule
source2: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline, 'Yuan Dynasty (1271-1368)' - https://www.metmuseum.org/toah/hd/yuan/hd_yuan.htm
notes: Rebellions from 1351 and regional states broke Yuan control; Nanjing-based rebel Ming (internal) took Dadu 1368; emperor and overthrown government fled north. Court survived in Mongolia (Northern Yuan), so T5 arguable.

source1: Jeremy B. Rutter, Aegean Prehistoric Archaeology, Lesson 29 'Post-Palatial Twilight: The Aegean in the Twelfth Century B.C.', Dartmouth College - https://sites.dartmouth.edu/aegean-prehistory/lessons/lesson-29-narrative/
source2: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline, 'Minoan Crete' - https://www.metmuseum.org/toah/hd/mino/hd_mino.htm
notes: Phase with no capital. LM IIIB-IIIC transition c.1200: unsettled conditions, shift to refuge sites (Karphi, Kavousi), Minoan culture continued declining into 11th c.; some mainland migrant influx proposed. LM IIIB Knossos/Chania administration debated.

successor: Roman Republic (province of Crete, later Crete and Cyrene)
source2: Velleius Paterculus, Roman History II.34 (trans. F. W. Shipley), LacusCurtius, University of Chicago - https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Velleius_Paterculus/2B*.html
notes: Independent poleis, no capital. Metellus (consul 69 BCE) conquered island over three years against 24,000 Cretans; annexed with Cyrene as province. Conquest completed 67 BCE, not 69. Intercity wars plausible but unverified for Q4.

source1: United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, Holocaust Encyclopedia, 'German Invasion of Western Europe, May 1940' - https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/german-invasion-of-western-europe-may-1940
notes: Germany invaded 10 May 1940; surrender 14 May; queen and government exiled to Britain (continued, restored 1945); Reichskommissar Seyss-Inquart ruled. Region 'Southern Europe' is wrong (Western Europe). Colonies held until 1942.

Later Zhou commander Zhao Kuangyin acclaimed by troops 960; officers spared imperial family and councillors; Taizu continued existing system. Database end 970 wrong (960). Khitan occupation of Kaifeng 947 temporary. Q4: repeated coups.

Rebel Ken Angrok (later Singhasari king) defeated Kadiri king Kertajaya at Ganter 1222; Singhasari replaced Kadiri, which became subordinate. Rebel internal, so not T2. Kadiri lay in eastern Java, not Central Java.

source2: Peoria Tribe of Indians of Oklahoma, 'History' - https://peoriatribe.com/history/
notes: Loose confederation of Algonquian tribes with village councils, no central authority; Kaskaskia and Peoria persisted after 1717, trading at Fort de Chartres (1720). 1717/18 break is periodisation. Iroquois raids (external) reduced numbers.
